solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: S American native prepared after second to seize weapon

indicators.note: 'after' places one piece behind the other in the answer's reading order
to seize something is to grab hold of it, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
an arm is a weapon, as in firearm
set means ready or prepared

explanation.surface: A native South American readies his weapon in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'S American native' looks like a person, but it is an animal. 'Half a mo' is British for a moment, so a second.
explanation.definitionFit: The marmoset is a small monkey found in the forests of South America, so it is native there.

clue.text: Daniel's companion, retired, gaining new self-confidence

parts.note: someone who has retired for the night is in bed, abed
N is the abbreviation for new
ego is a sense of self-worth

explanation.surface: A friend of someone called Daniel has retired and grown more self-assured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' suggests leaving work, but here it means gone to bed: ABED.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach and this man were thrown into the fiery furnace alongside the prophet's story.

clue.text: Folk I link with servility

parts.note: men are people, folk
taken as written
to ally is to link or join with

explanation.surface: Someone admits they associate ordinary people with servile behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Link' is a verb here: to ally oneself with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a lowly, servant-like manner is acting with servility, an adverb phrase matching the -ly ending.

clue.text: Trim tail off wader

indicators.note: taking the tail off removes the final letter of the word

parts.note: the snipe is a long-billed wading bird

explanation.surface: An instruction to clip the tail feathers off a wading bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A wader in crosswords is usually a wading bird, not a person in boots.
explanation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut a small piece off with scissors, which is to trim something.

clue.text: Racing home?

parts.note: surface reading: hurrying back to your house
setter's reading: where a branch of horse racing takes place, its name also meaning an apartment, a home

explanation.walkthrough: The clue suggests rushing home; really it asks for the home of one kind of horse racing, run without jumps, whose name is also a word for an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat racing, run over level ground without hurdles, is called this in Britain, and a flat is also a place to live.

clue.text: He made preparations to preach differently through a year

indicators.note: running through something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another
done differently means arranged another way, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
Y is the abbreviation for year
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clergyman got ready to vary his sermons over the course of a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preparations' suggests getting ready, but it means medicines made up. The rearranged letters sit between A and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: An apothecary was the old name for a pharmacist, who compounded and sold medicinal preparations.

clue.text: Very determined man will grass

parts.note: 'he will' contracts to he'll, with he standing for a man
bent is a type of grass

explanation.surface: A man so resolute he is going to inform on his associates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like the British slang verb 'to inform', but it is the plant. The apostrophe of HE'LL disappears in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Being set on something regardless of consequences means being fiercely determined, the idiom's everyday sense.

clue.text: Say, Iran's revised ancient Middle Eastern language

indicators.note: a revised text has been altered and reworked, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A remark that the version of a country's tongue has been updated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example', but its letters join the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The Akkadian dialect spoken in the empire of Nineveh and Ashur was this tongue of the ancient Near East.

clue.text: Terrible footballer's in short socks

indicators.note: 'in' puts one piece inside another
something cut short loses its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: hose is an old word for stockings or socks
Pelé was the great Brazilian footballer, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A dreadful football player turns out in skimpy socks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Footballer' in crosswords is very often the Brazilian great; the possessive S stays with his name inside the shortened socks.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without hope of success is useless, which matches the informal sense of terrible, very bad.

clue.text: For the moment I am facing my opposite

indicators.note: facing something means standing right in front of it, so one piece comes first

parts.note: 'I am' is the speaker identifying as me
something opposed to me is anti-me

explanation.surface: Someone describes confronting their own opposite for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: ME faces ANTI-ME, its opposite; the definition is the phrase 'in the meantime'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In the meantime' means for now, during the interval, so the noun covers the present period.

clue.text: Be entirely appropriate? Only at odd intervals

parts.note: fit means suitable or appropriate
fully means entirely

explanation.surface: A question whether something is quite right, answered with 'only occasionally'.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads 'be fit fully', with the two words swapped round so FIT comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in fits and starts means irregularly, happening only now and then with gaps between.

clue.text: What landlord has to say about beer to start with

indicators.note: something placed at the start goes in front, fixing which piece leads

parts.note: re means about or concerning
ale is a kind of beer
to state is to say

explanation.surface: A pub landlord's view on beer, offered right at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landlord' suggests a publican, but it is the owner of property; the beer pieces come first because of 'to start with'.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord owns land and buildings that are let out, which is property, the American term for it included.

clue.text: Rider to move quickly during downpour

indicators.note: during means within a period of time, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a shower is a fall of rain
to jump is to move suddenly and fast

explanation.surface: A horseman hurries along in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downpour' suggests heavy rain; the lighter word for a fall of rain is what wraps the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in equestrian events jumping fences in an arena rides a horse, so is one kind of rider.

clue.text: Where you may find some house mice?

definitions.text: Where you may find some house mice?

indicators.note: 'some' means only part of what follows, so the letters are taken from inside the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the word break

explanation.surface: A question about where mice might live.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a type of house holds some of the letters, and mice may live in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached house is a common British home, and any house is a place where mice can turn up.

clue.text: College once left almost 50p as an example

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a poly was a polytechnic, a British college type abolished in 1992
gone means left or departed

explanation.surface: A former college's leaver had almost fifty pence to their name.
explanation.walkthrough: The British 50p coin is a seven-sided shape; 'as an example' marks it as an instance of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifty-pence coin is a heptagon, a many-sided plane figure, so it is one example of that shape.

clue.text: CO picking up beret with one clenched hand

indicators.note: in a down clue picking up lifts a word so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a beret is a kind of cap
I is the Roman numeral one
a fist is a clenched hand

explanation.surface: A commanding officer lifts his beret with a clenched fist.
explanation.walkthrough: CO looks like commanding officer; it is a conscientious objector, one who refuses military service.
explanation.definitionFit: A conscientious objector refuses to fight on moral grounds, which is what someone opposed to war and violence does.

clue.text: Reformist leaders of local unit nervous around a certain regiment

indicators.note: around means enclosing, so one piece wraps another
leaders go at the front, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words
the RA is the Royal Artillery, a British regiment

explanation.surface: Reforming chiefs of a local army unit are nervous about a particular regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nervous' looks like a description but is just one of the three words supplying initials. 'A certain' gives THE.
explanation.definitionFit: The followers of Martin Luther formed a Protestant church out of the Reformation, so they are reformist.

clue.text: Turner does better with brown

parts.note: to cap something is to outdo it
tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: The painter Turner outdoes others in his use of brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' looks like the painter J. M. W. Turner, but it is anything that turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A capstan is a revolving drum on a ship used for winding cable, so it is a thing that rotates.

clue.text: Son making fun of ornamental stitching

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
mocking means ridiculing

explanation.surface: A boy ridicules some decorative needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: S plus MOCKING; 'of' belongs to the wordplay phrase rather than linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Smocking is decorative embroidery that gathers fabric into tight pleats, as on a traditional smock.

clue.text: What 6 maybe offered in repeat upset

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: What a chemist might hand over for a recurring stomach upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 refers to the answer at 6-down, APOTHECARY. 'Upset' fits the medical surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: A laxative is the kind of medicine an old chemist would supply, and this word names such a remedy.

clue.text: Spoils public library? Not on

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for public library
if not on top of something, it may be beneath it

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that spoiling the public library is not acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a verb but is the noun, and 'Not on' looks like British 'not acceptable' but means beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Plunder is goods seized by force or theft, the same as spoils or loot taken in war.

clue.text: Extremely important not to start appealing

indicators.note: not having a start means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: an acute need is a severe and critical one

explanation.surface: A warning that it is vital not to begin an appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appealing' looks like a legal appeal, but it is the adjective meaning attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: Something charming or sweet and pretty is attractive, which is what the adjective appealing means.

clue.text: Ensign's delight about pounds received

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: joy is delight
L is the abbreviation for a pound, doubled for the plural
in radio talk roger means message received

explanation.surface: A junior naval officer is thrilled to be paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ensign' looks like a junior officer but is a flag, and 'Ensign's' reads as 'Ensign is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull-and-crossbones flag flown by pirate ships is a naval flag, which an ensign is.

clue.text: Cheeky bloke only just up

parts.note: fresh can mean impudent or cheeky
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: An impudent fellow who has barely got out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only just up' sounds like just awake, but 'going up' is British for starting university; the definition is a noun phrase for a new student.
explanation.definitionFit: A first-year student has only recently come up to university, the traditional phrase for arriving there.

clue.text: No place for involving more than one river

indicators.note: 'no' says something is absent, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a plural form refers to more than one
PL is the abbreviation for place

explanation.surface: A sign saying a spot is off-limits to anything involving more than one river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involving more than one' describes a grammatical form, not a meeting of rivers; the abbreviation for place comes off its front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ural flows from the Ural Mountains through Russia and Kazakhstan into the Caspian Sea.

clue.text: Took a risk housing priest about to be thrown off course

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters read backwards
a house holds its occupant, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to dare is to take a risk
Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Someone gambled on a clergyman who was about to be knocked off track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to be' looks like 'on the point of', but 'about' reverses D(ELI)ARED.
explanation.definitionFit: A train that leaves its rails is knocked off its route, and figuratively plans are diverted from their path.

clue.text: Furious speed across carpet, turning back in panic

indicators.note: turning back means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
spread across something means stretching round it, so one piece encloses another
something furious is wild and frenzied, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
a mat is a small carpet

explanation.surface: Someone rushes across a carpet at high speed and spins round in alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Furious speed' reads as great haste, but 'Furious' only says to rearrange the letters of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden mass rush of frightened animals or people, a herd in panic.

clue.text: Sideline, say, going into recount

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: to relate a story is to recount it
e.g. means for example, which is what 'say' can mean

explanation.surface: An election official is pushed aside during a recount of votes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recount' suggests counting votes again, but here it means to tell a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To relegate someone is to demote them to a lesser position, pushing them out of the main action.
